items.question: Assess the achievements of Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) as the greatest of the Pallava kings, with special reference to his conflict with the Chalukyas and his contribution to art at Mamallapuram.
items.modelAnswer:
**Narasimhavarman I 'Mamalla' (630–668 CE)** is regarded as the **greatest Pallava king**, combining decisive military success with an enduring artistic legacy.

**Military achievements:** He avenged his father Mahendravarman I — who had been killed by **Pulakeshin II at the Battle of Pullalur** — by **defeating and slaying Pulakeshin II and destroying the Chalukya capital Vatapi (Badami)**, earning the title **Vatapikonda ('Conqueror of Vatapi')**. He also projected Pallava power overseas, **invading Sri Lanka twice** to restore the exiled prince **Manavamma**. His court's prestige is reflected in his **hosting of the Chinese pilgrim Hsuen Tsang at Kanchipuram in 642 CE**.

**Art and architecture:** Narasimhavarman I **founded Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram)** and initiated the **Seven Rathas** — monolithic chariot-shrines (Draupadi, Dharmaraja, Bhima Rathas) that define the **Mamalla Style**, marked by **rock-cut mandapas and lion-headed pillars**. These works, later crowned by the Shore Temple of his successor, made Mamallapuram a **UNESCO World Heritage** ensemble and a foundation of the **Dravidian temple tradition**.

**Assessment:** By fusing **victory over the Chalukyas, overseas influence, and pioneering monolithic architecture**, Narasimhavarman I embodies the zenith of Pallava power and remains central to the cultural history of south India.
keyPoints: Avenged Pullalur; defeated and killed Pulakeshin II and destroyed Vatapi — title Vatapikonda.
Invaded Sri Lanka twice to restore the exiled prince Manavamma.
Hosted Hsuen Tsang at Kanchipuram in 642 CE.
Founded Mamallapuram; initiated the Seven Rathas (Mamalla Style).
Rock-cut mandapas and lion-headed pillars; foundation of Dravidian architecture and a UNESCO site.

items.question: Trace the course and significance of the Pallava–Chalukya conflict in post-Gupta south India, using the Aihole inscription as a key source.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Pallavas of Kanchi** and the **Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi)** were the two dominant powers of post-Gupta south India, and their prolonged rivalry shaped Deccan and Tamil politics for over a century.

**Course of the conflict:** The struggle opened when **Pulakeshin II**, the greatest Chalukya, **defeated and killed Mahendravarman I at the Battle of Pullalur**. The Pallavas struck back decisively under **Narasimhavarman I**, who **defeated and slew Pulakeshin II and sacked Vatapi**, taking the title **Vatapikonda**. Hostilities continued intermittently — the Chalukyan army at one point **plundered Kanchipuram** — before subsiding under **Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha)**, whose reign was marked by peace.

**The Aihole inscription:** Composed by Pulakeshin II's Jain court poet **Ravikirti**, the **Aihole prashasti** is the principal source for Chalukyan power. It records Pulakeshin's conquests, including his celebrated **check on Harshavardhana at the Narmada**, and exemplifies the age's polished Sanskrit eulogy.

**Significance:** The rivalry (a) drained both powers militarily, contributing to the eventual **Pallava decline before the Cholas** under **Aditya I**; (b) spurred **competitive temple-building** — Pallava Dravidian temples at Mamallapuram and Kanchi, and Chalukyan monuments at **Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal** that fed the **Vesara style**; and (c) makes the epigraphs of the period, above all the Aihole inscription, indispensable to reconstructing early medieval south Indian history.
keyPoints: Pulakeshin II killed Mahendravarman I at Pullalur; Narasimhavarman I retaliated by sacking Vatapi.
Chalukyas later plundered Kanchipuram; conflict subsided under Rajasimha.
Aihole inscription by Ravikirti records Pulakeshin II's deeds, incl. checking Harsha at the Narmada.
Rivalry drained both powers and hastened Pallava decline before the Cholas (Aditya I).
Fostered competitive temple-building: Pallava Dravidian vs Chalukyan Badami/Aihole/Pattadakal (Vesara).

items.question: Examine the contribution of the Pallavas to temple architecture and to institutions of local self-government in south India.
items.modelAnswer:
The Pallavas of Kanchi were pioneers both in **temple architecture** and in the **institutions of village self-government**, laying foundations later perfected by the Cholas.

**Temple architecture — the birth of the Dravidian style:** Pallava building evolved through four phases. The **Mahendra Style** (Mahendravarman I) introduced the earliest **rock-cut temples**, using no brick or wood (Mamandur, Trimurti Mandapa). The **Mamalla Style** (Narasimhavarman I) added **monolithic Rathas** and **lion-headed pillars** at Mamallapuram. The **Rajasimha Style** (Narasimhavarman II) shifted to elaborate **structural temples** in stone — the **Shore Temple** and the **Kailashnath Temple** (with its 16-sided Shivalinga and 58 devakulikas). The final **Nandivarman Style** produced smaller temples such as the **Vaikunth Perumal**, reflecting decline. Together these define the **Dravidian (vimana) tradition**, distinct from the northern **Nagara** and Deccan **Vesara** styles, and preserve painting at **Chittannavasal**.

**Local self-government:** The Pallava state, a **monarchy** under kings styled **Dharma-Maharaja**, was divided into **Kottams** under royal officers. Below this, **villages functioned as self-governing republics** managed by assemblies — the **Sabha** (Brahmadeya villages) and the **Urar** (ordinary villages) — with a village court, the **Dharmasasana**, for justice. Economic institutions such as **Brahmadeya** grants, merchant guilds (**Manigramam**) and **Eripatti** (tank lands) supported this order.

**Conclusion:** Through the Dravidian temple form and a mature system of village autonomy, the Pallavas created cultural and administrative templates that the Cholas inherited and elevated — securing their lasting place in south Indian history.
keyPoints: Four architectural phases: Mahendra (rock-cut) → Mamalla (Rathas) → Rajasimha (structural) → Nandivarman (decline).
Landmark temples: Shore Temple, Kailashnath (16-sided Shivalinga, 58 devakulikas), Vaikunth Perumal.
Founded the Dravidian (vimana) style; contrast with Nagara and Vesara; Chittannavasal frescoes.
Monarchy (Dharma-Maharaja) over Kottams; villages self-governed by Sabha and Urar; Dharmasasana courts.
Economic supports: Brahmadeya grants, Manigramam guilds, Eripatti tank lands — templates inherited by the Cholas.
